chapters.customSummary:
- Migration testing checks complete, no extras/duplicates, accurate, consistent, traceable (rejects), and usable; errors are silent and often surface weeks later.
- Start from the mapping spec (each rule is a test) and ask about anything it doesn't say (single-word names, unknown departments).
- Row counts are not enough: 6 = 6 + 0 rejects looked fine while only 5 distinct keys arrived. Reconcile distinct business keys.
- Control totals (count, sums, min/max dates, distinct counts, non-NULL counts) are a smoke alarm only: salary total was off by 5,000, but min/max dates missed the date swap.
- Key-level completeness in both directions (lost, invented) plus duplicates by key.
- Field-level diff: apply the mapping to the source in SQL and compare to the target with NULL-safe operators; output expected vs actual per column (caught date swap, wrong status, trailing space; the duplicate needs the key check).
- Ambiguous dates: test day > 12 and day <= 12, leap days, NULL, malformed text.
- Row hashes (MD5(CONCAT_WS(...)) with COALESCE, since CONCAT_WS skips NULLs) speed up wide-table comparison and work across servers.
- Test each transformation with edge data (name splits, every status code, department lookup, trim/case, money precision); list unmapped values.
- Target integrity: orphans, business-key uniqueness, and missing UNIQUE constraints (loads often disable checks).
- Rejects: reasons must be logged and allowed; a row in neither target nor reject log is a silent loss (Kiran).
- Check narrowing (lengths, precision, charset, time zones, encoding); silent truncation in non-strict mode.
- Idempotency (run twice, compare), incremental loads, timing, and UI smoke via Playwright/Selenium using toHaveCount(1) to catch missing and duplicated records.
- Cross-server: per-key hashes plus counts compared in code (dicts hide duplicates). Prefer full-population comparison; sample the UI stratified by risk.
- Report findings with evidence and severity; the run had 5 defects behind matching counts.
chapters.contentMarkdown:
## Migration testing is its own discipline
A migration moves data from one place to another: an old system into a new one, one schema into a restructured schema, an Excel import into the HRMS, or a nightly ETL job feeding a reporting database. It differs from ordinary feature testing in three ways. It runs once (or rarely), at scale, so you can't fix it by clicking "save" again. Errors are silent, since a wrong date or a lost row throws no exception. And the damage often surfaces weeks later, when payroll pays the wrong person or a resigned employee can log in. Correct migration means six things: everything arrived (complete), nothing extra arrived (no extras or duplicates), every value is right after transformation (accurate), the relationships still hold (consistent), rejected data is accounted for (traceable), and the new system actually works with it (usable). Each layer below checks one or more of these, and every layer catches things the previous ones miss.
## Start from the mapping specification
You can't verify a transformation you haven't read. Before running any query, get the mapping document (or write it down with the analyst) and turn it into a table like this one:

| Target column | Source | Rule |
|---|---|---|
| legacy_emp_no | emp_no | Copy, must be unique in target |
| first_name | full_name | Text before the first space |
| last_name | full_name | Text after the last space |
| email | email | Trim spaces, lowercase |
| department_id | dept_name | Look up by name in departments; unknown name is a reject |
| hire_date | join_date | Parse DD-MM-YYYY into a DATE |
| status | status_code | A to active, I to inactive, R to resigned; other codes are rejects |
| basic_salary | salary | Copy, no rounding |

Every row of this table is a test. Anything the spec doesn't say (what happens to a single-word name, or to an unknown department?) is a question to ask before you sign off.
## Layer 1: row counts, and why they are not enough
The first check everyone runs is "do the counts match?", and it should include the reject log if the tool has one. The reconciliation identity is source rows = loaded rows + rejected rows:
```sql
SELECT (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM legacy_employees)                        AS src_rows,
       (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM mig_employees)                           AS tgt_rows,
       (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM mig_rejects)                             AS rejected,
       (SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT legacy_emp_no) FROM mig_employees)      AS tgt_distinct_keys;
```

src_rows | tgt_rows | rejected | tgt_distinct_keys
6        | 6        | 0        | 5

The identity holds (6 = 6 + 0), and the migration "passes" a count check. Yet the last column shows only five distinct source employees made it across. A duplicate offset a loss, so the row counts agreed while the content did not. The lesson is to reconcile distinct business keys, and never trust a row count alone. If you are asked to sign off on "counts match," ask "counts of what?"
## Layer 2: control totals
Control totals are cheap aggregates computed identically on both sides: row count, sum of every money column, min and max of every date, distinct counts of natural keys, and counts of non-NULL values per column. They catch bulk problems fast and give you numbers you can paste into a test report.
```sql
SELECT 'source' AS side,
```
| COUNT(*)                                       AS row_cnt, | SUM(salary)                                    AS total_salary, | MIN(STR_TO_DATE(join_date, '%d-%m-%Y'))        AS min_date, | MAX(STR_TO_DATE(join_date, '%d-%m-%Y'))        AS max_date, | COUNT(DISTINCT LOWER(TRIM(email)))             AS distinct_emails |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| FROM   legacy_employees | UNION ALL | SELECT 'target', COUNT(*), SUM(basic_salary), MIN(hire_date), MAX(hire_date), | COUNT(DISTINCT LOWER(TRIM(email))) | FROM   mig_employees; |

side   | row_cnt | total_salary | min_date   | max_date   | distinct_emails
source | 6       | 295000.00    | 2022-01-20 | 2025-09-01 | 6
## target | 6       | 300000.00    | 2022-01-20 | 2025-09-01 | 5

Now two signals appear: the salary total is off by 5,000 (Ravi's duplicated 45,000 minus Kiran's missing 40,000) and the distinct email count dropped from 6 to 5. But min_date and max_date match perfectly even though Asha's date is wrong, because a day/month swap moves a date without leaving the overall range. That is why control totals are a smoke alarm and never proof: a passing total says nothing about rows that changed in offsetting ways. You always need the deeper layers.
## Layer 3: key-level completeness
Compare the sets of business keys in both directions. This is the anti-join from 4.1 applied across systems:
-- In source, not in target (lost)
| SELECT l.emp_no, l.full_name | FROM   legacy_employees l |
|---|---|
| LEFT JOIN mig_employees m ON m.legacy_emp_no = l.emp_no | WHERE  m.mig_id IS NULL; |

-- In target, not in source (invented)
| SELECT m.mig_id, m.legacy_emp_no | FROM   mig_employees m |
|---|---|
| LEFT JOIN legacy_employees l ON l.emp_no = m.legacy_emp_no | WHERE  l.emp_no IS NULL; |

-- Loaded more than once
```sql
SELECT legacy_emp_no, COUNT(*) AS copies
FROM   mig_employees
GROUP  BY legacy_emp_no
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;
```

emp_no | full_name
1006   | Kiran Magar

(second query: 0 rows)

legacy_emp_no | copies
1002          | 2

These find the lost employee and the duplicate that the counts hid. The second query is the "extras" direction, which people forget. It finds rows that shouldn't exist at all (test accounts, rows from a previous run).
## Layer 4: field-level comparison against the transformed source
Complete keys don't prove correct values. The strongest technique is to apply the mapping rules to the source in SQL and compare the result to the target column by column, keyed on the business key. Compare the transformed source to the target with a NULL-safe operator (<=> in MySQL, IS NOT DISTINCT FROM in PostgreSQL and SQL Server 2022+), since a plain = skips rows where both sides are NULL (2.3, 4.1).

| WITH src AS ( | SELECT l.emp_no, |
|---|---|
| SUBSTRING_INDEX(l.full_name, ' ', 1)   AS first_name, | SUBSTRING_INDEX(l.full_name, ' ', -1)  AS last_name, |
| LOWER(TRIM(l.email))                   AS email, | d.department_id, |
| STR_TO_DATE(l.join_date, '%d-%m-%Y')   AS hire_date, | CASE l.status_code WHEN 'A' THEN 'active' WHEN 'I' THEN 'inactive' |
| WHEN 'R' THEN 'resigned' END AS status, | l.salary |
| FROM   legacy_employees l | LEFT JOIN departments d ON d.name = l.dept_name |
| ) | SELECT s.emp_no, 'hire_date' AS column_name, |
| CAST(s.hire_date AS CHAR) AS expected, CAST(m.hire_date AS CHAR) AS actual | FROM   src s JOIN mig_employees m ON m.legacy_emp_no = s.emp_no |
| WHERE  NOT (s.hire_date <=> m.hire_date) | UNION ALL |
| SELECT s.emp_no, 'status', s.status, CAST(m.status AS CHAR) | FROM   src s JOIN mig_employees m ON m.legacy_emp_no = s.emp_no |
| WHERE  NOT (s.status <=> m.status) | UNION ALL |
| SELECT s.emp_no, 'email', CONCAT('[', s.email, ']'), CONCAT('[', m.email, ']') | FROM   src s JOIN mig_employees m ON m.legacy_emp_no = s.emp_no |
| WHERE  NOT (s.email <=> m.email) | ORDER  BY emp_no, column_name; |

| emp_no \| column_name \| expected             \| actual | 1001   \| hire_date   \| 2024-03-01           \| 2024-01-03 |
|---|---|
| 1004   \| status      \| resigned             \| active | 1005   \| email       \| [bikash@example.com] \| [bikash@example.com ] |

In a real run you add one block per mapped column (first name, last name, department, salary). The output format is deliberately a diff, one row per wrong value with the expected and actual side by side, which is exactly what a defect report needs. Three details matter:
The square brackets around the email make invisible trailing whitespace visible (2.5).
Three defects surfaced here that no count or total detected: a date swap, a wrong status mapping and a whitespace slip.
The duplicate (1002) did not show up, because both copies carry correct values. Each layer has blind spots, which is why you stack them.
Ambiguous dates deserve special test data. A day/month swap is only silent when the day is 12 or less, because 15-07-2023 swapped becomes month 15 and either errors or is rejected. Asha's 01-03-2024 becoming 2024-01-03 is valid either way. So your source test data must include dates with day > 12 (which expose parse failures) and dates with day <= 12 (which expose silent swaps). Also try 29 February, dates at the ends of the range, and a NULL or blank date if the source permits them. If dates are text in the source, look for values that aren't dates at all: WHERE STR_TO_DATE(join_date, '%d-%m-%Y') IS NULL.
## Layer 5: row hashes for wide tables
Comparing 40 columns one by one is tedious. Compute a hash of the mapped columns on each side and compare only the hashes, then drill into the rows that differ:
```sql
WITH src AS ( /* same CTE as above */ ),
s AS (SELECT emp_no,
             MD5(CONCAT_WS('|', first_name, last_name, email, COALESCE(department_id, '<NULL>'),
```
| hire_date, status, salary)) AS h | FROM src), |
|---|---|
| t AS (SELECT legacy_emp_no AS emp_no, | MD5(CONCAT_WS('\|', first_name, last_name, email, COALESCE(department_id, '<NULL>'), |
| hire_date, status, basic_salary)) AS h | FROM mig_employees) |
| SELECT s.emp_no | FROM   s JOIN t ON t.emp_no = s.emp_no |
| WHERE  s.h <> t.h | ORDER  BY s.emp_no; |

| emp_no | 1001 |
|---|---|
| 1004 | 1005 |

Note the COALESCE, because CONCAT_WS silently skips NULL arguments (2.4), so ('a', NULL, 'b') and ('a', 'b') would hash the same. Use a delimiter that can't occur in the data. Hashing is also how you compare across servers, where you can't join tables directly: compute per-key hashes on each side and compare them in code (below).
## Layer 6: test each transformation rule with targeted data
The queries above check whatever data happened to be there. For each rule in the mapping spec, also check the edge cases the real data might not contain:

| Rule | Cases to plant in the source or check |
|---|---|
| Name split | Single word (Madonna), three parts (Mary Ann Smith, is Ann a middle name?), extra spaces, apostrophes, Devanagari, 50-plus characters |
| Status mapping | Every code (A, I, R), a lowercase code, a blank, an unknown code (X); is it rejected or defaulted? |
| Department lookup | Name with different case or trailing space, a department that doesn't exist, a NULL department |
| Date parse | Day > 12, day <= 12, leap day, NULL, malformed text |
| Trim/lowercase | Leading/trailing spaces, non-breaking space, mixed-case email |
| Money | 2 decimals, 0, a very large value, more than 2 decimals (rounded or rejected?) |

Many of these show up as unmapped values in the source, and you can list them before or after the load:
-- Source rows whose department name has no match in the target lookup (should each be a reject)
| SELECT l.emp_no, l.dept_name | FROM   legacy_employees l |
|---|---|
| LEFT JOIN departments d ON d.name = l.dept_name | WHERE  d.department_id IS NULL;                 -- 0 rows here |

-- Status codes the mapping doesn't know
```sql
SELECT status_code, COUNT(*) FROM legacy_employees
WHERE  status_code NOT IN ('A', 'I', 'R') GROUP BY status_code;   -- 0 rows
```

Notice that SUBSTRING_INDEX(full_name, ' ', -1) gives Ann Smith a last name of Smith and silently drops Ann from the last name only if the developer uses the same logic. Whether that's right is a business question, and the mapping spec has to answer it. Your job is to find the case, run it, and ask.
## Layer 7: integrity of the target
After the load, the target must obey its own rules. Re-run the orphan scoreboard from 4.3 and the uniqueness checks from 3.2 on the migrated tables. This matters especially because bulk loads often disable checks:
```sql
SELECT COUNT(*) AS orphan_departments
FROM   mig_employees m
LEFT JOIN departments d ON d.department_id = m.department_id
WHERE  m.department_id IS NOT NULL AND d.department_id IS NULL;   -- 0
```

-- Business uniqueness that the schema forgot to enforce
```sql
SELECT LOWER(TRIM(email)) AS email, COUNT(*) FROM mig_employees GROUP BY LOWER(TRIM(email)) HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;
```

The second query returns ravi@example.com with 2. The same table has no UNIQUE on legacy_emp_no or email, which is why the duplicate loaded, so the design gap deserves its own finding (8.1).
## Layer 8: rejects and logs
Every migration tool rejects some rows (bad dates, missing mandatory fields). Test three things about rejects: each rejected row appears in the reject log with a reason; the reject reasons are the ones the spec allows; and the reconciliation identity from Layer 1 holds by distinct key. If the tool only writes a log file, load it into a scratch table. A row that is in neither the target nor the reject log is a silent loss, the worst outcome, and Kiran is exactly that: absent from mig_employees and absent from mig_rejects.
## Layer 9: types, lengths, encoding and precision
Compare column definitions on both sides for narrowing: VARCHAR(100) into VARCHAR(50), DECIMAL(12,4) into DECIMAL(10,2), DATETIME into DATE, or a wider charset into a narrower one. Then look for the actual data at risk:
```sql
SELECT MAX(CHAR_LENGTH(full_name)) AS longest_source_name FROM legacy_employees;   -- must fit the target column
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM legacy_employees WHERE full_name <> TRIM(full_name);           -- padded values
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM legacy_employees WHERE LENGTH(full_name) <> CHAR_LENGTH(full_name);  -- multi-byte text present
```

In non-strict mode MySQL truncates silently, so a 60-character name loaded into VARCHAR(50) arrives cut off with no error (1.2). Check money for rounding (SUM and per-row comparisons at full precision), time zones (a source in local time landing in a UTC column shifts attendance punches by hours and can move a date across midnight), and encoding (Devanagari names arriving as ???? or as double-encoded garbage; 2.5).
## Layer 10: re-runs, incremental loads, timing, and the application
Ask what happens if the migration runs twice. A safe (idempotent) migration leaves the target unchanged on the second run, and an unsafe one doubles every row, which is very likely how Ravi got duplicated. Test on a clone: run it, capture control totals, run it again, compare. For incremental (delta) loads, change one source row, add one, delete one, and confirm the next run applies exactly those three changes and nothing else. Record how long the load takes on realistic volume, since the cutover window depends on it.
Finally test through the application, because a database can look perfect and still fail in the UI (a status value the front end doesn't know, a date format the API can't serialise). Sample a spread of migrated records across the risky categories (every status, oldest and newest hire dates, longest names, Devanagari names, employees with and without managers) and compare what the user sees with what the legacy system held:
```ts
import mysql from 'mysql2/promise';
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';
```

```ts
const STATUS_LABEL: Record<string, string> = { A: 'Active', I: 'Inactive', R: 'Resigned' };
```

```ts
test('migrated employees show the right status and hire date', async ({ page }) => {
  const legacy = await mysql.createConnection(process.env.LEGACY_DB_URL!);
  const [rows]: any = await legacy.execute(
    `SELECT emp_no, email, status_code, DATE_FORMAT(STR_TO_DATE(join_date,'%d-%m-%Y'),'%d %b %Y') AS hired
     FROM legacy_employees ORDER BY emp_no`);
  await legacy.end();
```

| for (const r of rows) { | await page.goto(`/employees?search=${encodeURIComponent(r.email)}`); |
|---|---|
| const row = page.getByRole('row', { name: new RegExp(r.email, 'i') }); | await expect(row, `employee ${r.emp_no} missing in UI`).toHaveCount(1);          // present, and only once |
| await expect(row.getByTestId('status')).toHaveText(STATUS_LABEL[r.status_code]); | await expect(row.getByTestId('hire-date')).toHaveText(r.hired); |
| } | }); |

The toHaveCount(1) assertion catches both the missing employee (count 0) and the duplicate (count 2). The equivalent Selenium version loops over the same query with driver.find_elements(By.XPATH, ...) and asserts len(...) == 1.
## When the two systems live on different servers
You can't JOIN across servers. Compute a key and a hash per row on each side and compare in code. Keep the counts too, because a dictionary silently collapses duplicate keys:

| def fetch(conn, sql): | with conn.cursor() as cur: |
|---|---|
| cur.execute(sql) | return cur.fetchall() |

src_rows = fetch(legacy_conn, """SELECT emp_no, MD5(CONCAT_WS('|', ...)) FROM legacy_employees""")
## tgt_rows = fetch(new_conn,    """SELECT legacy_emp_no, MD5(CONCAT_WS('|', ...)), COUNT(*)
                                 FROM mig_employees GROUP BY legacy_emp_no, 2""")

src = {k: h for k, h in src_rows}
tgt = {k: (h, n) for k, h, n in tgt_rows}

| missing   = sorted(src.keys() - tgt.keys()) | extra     = sorted(tgt.keys() - src.keys()) |
|---|---|
| changed   = sorted(k for k in src.keys() & tgt.keys() if src[k] != tgt[k][0]) | duplicated = sorted(k for k, (_, n) in tgt.items() if n > 1) |

## assert not (missing or extra or changed or duplicated), \
## f"missing={missing} extra={extra} changed={changed} duplicated={duplicated}"

For this data it would report missing=[1006] changed=[1001, 1004, 1005] duplicated=[1002]. Dedicated tools do the same job (DBeaver's data compare, pt-table-checksum, Python's datacompy), but the SQL version needs nothing installed and is easy to attach to a bug report.
## Full population beats sampling
If both sides are reachable, compare every row with set-based SQL, since a query costs the same whether it checks 6 rows or 6 million. Reserve sampling for the UI layer, where each check is slow, and stratify the sample by risk (each status, extremes, special characters) instead of taking random rows. A random sample of 20 rows out of 5,000 will very likely miss the one employee with a Devanagari name and a leap-day hire date.
Reporting the outcome
The findings for this migration, in report form:
| # | Finding | Evidence | Severity |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Employee 1006 lost | Absent from target and from reject log | High |
| 2 | Employee 1002 loaded twice | 2 rows for the key; salary total inflated by 45,000 | High |
| 3 | Employee 1001 hire date day/month swapped | 2024-03-01 became 2024-01-03 | High (tenure, leave) |
| 4 | Employee 1004 status wrong | R mapped to active (a resigned person can log in) | Critical |
| 5 | Employee 1005 email has trailing space | Breaks login and matching | Medium |
| 6 | Root cause candidates | No UNIQUE on legacy_emp_no/email; migration not idempotent | Design |

Note that the row count matched from the start. A sign-off based on that check alone would have shipped five defects. Chapter 11.3 covers packaging query results as evidence, and 12.3 turns a checklist like this into a reusable suite.

chapters.contentMarkdown:
## The core loop of data testing
Almost every data check has the same shape: obtain the result the system should produce, obtain what it actually produced, and compare them completely and mechanically. 6.1 did it for a migration, and this chapter generalises it: payroll runs against the analyst's calculation, an export against the screen, a report against the raw tables, a new release's output against the last release's. The skill is doing it in a way that finds every difference and never invents false ones.

| Where "expected" comes from | Source |
|---|---|
| Trust | Caveat |
| The requirement or spec, worked out by hand | High |
| Small samples only | An analyst's spreadsheet or calculation |
| High, but they make mistakes too | Check their rounding and rules |
| The old system's output | Medium |
| It may itself be wrong, so treat differences as questions | An independent SQL calculation you wrote |
| High | It must not share the app's logic or bugs |
| A previous release's output (baseline) | Medium |
| Proves no change, not correctness | A known seed data set with hand-verified answers |
| Very high | Limited coverage |

The most important rule is that the oracle must be independent of the code under test. If you copy the developer's formula into your query, you'll reproduce their bug and pass. Derive expected values from the requirement (basic + allowances - deductions) and not from reading the code.
## Getting expected data into the database
Comparison is easiest when both sides are tables, so load the expected data into a scratch table. From a CSV:
```sql
-- MySQL (local_infile must be enabled on server and client)
```
| LOAD DATA LOCAL INFILE '/tmp/expected_payroll_aug.csv' | INTO TABLE expected_payroll_aug |
|---|---|
| FIELDS TERMINATED BY ',' OPTIONALLY ENCLOSED BY '"' LINES TERMINATED BY '\n' IGNORE 1 LINES; | -- PostgreSQL (psql):   \copy expected_payroll_aug FROM 'expected_payroll_aug.csv' CSV HEADER |
| -- SQL Server:          BULK INSERT expected_payroll_aug FROM 'C:\data\expected.csv' | --                      WITH (FIRSTROW = 2, FIELDTERMINATOR = ',', ROWTERMINATOR = '\n'); |

DBeaver's import wizard does the same with a GUI. Type the columns properly (DECIMAL, DATE) so the comparison isn't text against numbers (1.2). On a read-only account where you can't create tables, embed the expected values inline as a CTE:
```sql
-- MySQL 8.0.19+
WITH expected (employee_id, net_pay) AS (VALUES ROW(1, 57500), ROW(2, 43500), ROW(3, 67000))
SELECT * FROM expected;
-- PostgreSQL:  (VALUES (1, 57500), (2, 43500)) AS expected(employee_id, net_pay)
```

## Choose the comparison key first
Decide what identifies "the same record" on both sides: employee_id, or (employee_id, pay_month), or (legacy_emp_no). Everything else is compared column by column for the same key. A wrong key produces nonsense: keying payroll on employee_id alone across several months matches every month against every other.
## Classify every record: MATCH, DIFF, MISSING, DUPLICATE, EXTRA
A single query can classify all expected records (window functions from 5.5 help detect duplicates):

| WITH actual AS ( | SELECT p.*, | COUNT(*)     OVER (PARTITION BY employee_id)                      AS copies, |
|---|---|---|

## Normalise before comparing
Many false differences come from comparing values that mean the same thing but look different. Decide the rules and apply them to both sides:

| Value type | Normalise by | Example | Money | Compare within a tolerance, or round both to the required scale | ABS(a.net_pay - e.net_pay) < 0.01 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Text | TRIM, LOWER, and remove non-breaking spaces if imports are involved (2.5) | LOWER(TRIM(a.email)) = LOWER(TRIM(e.email)) | Dates and times | Agree on time zone and precision; truncate seconds if the UI hides them | DATE(a.created_at), or compare in UTC |
| Codes vs labels | Map one side to the other | 'A' vs 'Active' | Booleans | Map 0/1, true/false, Y/N to one form | is_deleted = 1 vs "Yes" |
| Ordering | Sort both sides on a total order before comparing lists | ORDER BY employee_id | NULL vs empty | Decide whether '' equals NULL | NULLIF(TRIM(x), '') |

Tolerances are a judgement, so write them into the test report ("differences under 0.01 ignored, per requirement R-114"). A tolerance you adopt silently to make a test pass is how real rounding defects get buried. Rounding rules themselves (SQL versus Python versus JavaScript) are in 2.4.

The same approach works when the "actual" is something other than a table. Pull the actual data from the UI, the API response or an exported file into a list of records, load the expected side from SQL, and compare by key. ## both    = m[m["_merge"] == "both"]

Two subtle problems: DECIMAL values arrive as strings from many drivers (3.1), so cast before comparing; and exports often format numbers (57,500.00), so strip the formatting on the UI side, never on the database side.
## Comparing two versions of the same query or environment
When a query is rewritten (a report is optimised, a view is refactored), the old version is your oracle: old EXCEPT new and new EXCEPT old must both be empty. The same trick works across environments or releases (6.5 and 6.6): run the identical query in two places and diff the results.
## Report the differences usefully
A comparison result is only helpful if someone can act on it. Include the key, the column, the expected value, the actual value, and the difference for numbers. Summarise counts by category (1 match, 1 duplicate, 1 diff, 1 missing), keep the full list as an attachment (11.3), and record which comparison rules and tolerances you used.
## Pitfalls to avoid
Comparing a result with itself. Computing "expected" from the same table (or the same view) the app reads proves nothing.
Hidden duplicates. Set-based comparison hides them; check counts too (copies above).
Type mismatches. A '57500.00' string does not equal 57500 in strict tests, and Decimal('0.1') isn't 0.1 as a float.
Unstable order. Comparing two lists position by position without a total ORDER BY produces random failures (2.2).
Stale expected data. When the requirement changes, the spreadsheet changes; keep a version and a date with every expected file.
Silent tolerance. If more than a few rows need a tolerance to pass, the rounding rule itself may be the defect.

chapters.contentMarkdown:
## Three families of problems that constraints don't catch
Databases enforce rules that someone remembered to declare. Everything else is left to the application, and applications have bugs. Three kinds of damage keep recurring in real HRMS data: duplicates (records that should be unique appear more than once), orphans (records that refer to something that isn't there), and mismatched counts (numbers that should agree don't). They arise from double clicks, retried API calls, imports, migrations, partial failures, deletes that don't clean up, and code that updates one table but not the other. Each has a standard query pattern, and this chapter pulls them together into one suite.
Duplicates: decide what "duplicate" means first
There are three levels, and each needs a different query.
Exact duplicates: every column identical, except the surrogate key. The classic result of a double submit.
Business-key duplicates: the columns that should be unique repeat, while other columns may differ. Two payroll rows for the same employee and month, two attendance rows for the same day, two migrated rows for the same legacy ID.
Near duplicates: the same real-world thing entered slightly differently: Asha@Example.com and asha@example.com , or Ravi Shrestha and Ravi Shrestha.
The GROUP BY ... HAVING COUNT(*) > 1 pattern from 3.2 finds the first two, and normalising inside the GROUP BY finds the third:
-- Business-key duplicates (payroll)
```sql
SELECT employee_id, pay_month, COUNT(*) AS copies
FROM   payroll GROUP BY employee_id, pay_month HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;
-- employee 2, 2026-08-01, 2
```

-- Near duplicates (normalised email in the migrated table)
```sql
SELECT LOWER(TRIM(email)) AS normalised_email, COUNT(*) AS copies, GROUP_CONCAT(mig_id) AS mig_ids
FROM   mig_employees
GROUP  BY LOWER(TRIM(email))
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;
```

normalised_email | copies | mig_ids
## ravi@example.com | 2      | 2,3

To list every copy with its details (what a bug report needs), use a window count (5.5) instead of collapsing the rows:
```sql
WITH d AS (
  SELECT m.*, COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY legacy_emp_no) AS copies
  FROM   mig_employees m
)
SELECT mig_id, legacy_emp_no, first_name, last_name, copies FROM d WHERE copies > 1;
```

mig_id | legacy_emp_no | first_name | last_name | copies
2      | 1002          | Ravi       | Shrestha  | 2
3      | 1002          | Ravi       | Shrestha  | 2

Before reporting, ask whether the repeat is really wrong. Two leave requests for identical dates might be a legitimate re-application after a rejection, and two attendance rows could be a valid split shift. The business key encodes the rule. Add a strict created_at comparison too: rows created within a second of each other are usually a double click, and rows created days apart are usually a different event. Note the fix as well as the data: a duplicate that could get in means the UNIQUE constraint is missing (8.1), and your test should also try to create it through the UI and API (double-click the Save button, replay the API call twice) and check the outcome.
## Orphans: a recap and some new shapes
Section 4.3 built the full method (constraint check, anti-join scoreboard, logical orphans, completeness, delta assertions). The essentials: LEFT JOIN ... WHERE parent.key IS NULL for hard orphans, extra conditions for soft-deleted or inactive parents, and the mirror image for parents that should have children. Other places orphans hide:
Audit and history rows whose changed_by points at a deleted user, and leave_status_history rows whose request no longer exists.
Polymorphic references, where entity_type and entity_id columns point at different tables depending on the type, and no foreign key can be declared: check each type's ids against its own table.
Files and attachments: rows pointing at a file path that no longer exists on disk or in object storage, and files with no row (this needs a script, since SQL can't see the file system).
Denormalised copies, such as a department_name copied into an employee row that no longer matches the department table (that leans into mismatched counts and values, below).
## Mismatched counts: five kinds
A "count mismatch" is any pair of numbers that the business says must agree. Recognising the type tells you how to look.
1. Source versus target. The migration case. Compare distinct keys, not rows (6.1).
2. Parent versus child totals. A header row that stores or implies a count of its children. If an order has item_count = 3 but 2 item rows exist, something failed midway.
-- Pattern: stored counter vs actual children
```sql
SELECT h.id, h.item_count AS stored, COUNT(c.id) AS actual
FROM   header h LEFT JOIN child c ON c.header_id = h.id
GROUP  BY h.id, h.item_count
HAVING h.item_count <> COUNT(c.id);
```

3. The UI, API and database triangle. A dashboard tile, the API total and the database COUNT(*) should agree, given the same filters. If two agree and one doesn't, the odd one out points at the layer to investigate. Common causes are a UI that counts only the loaded page, an API that forgets a soft-delete filter, and a database query that includes rows the UI hides.
4. Stored versus recomputed values. A stored figure that can be recomputed independently from the raw rows: leave days from the date range and the working calendar, net_pay from its components (Part 2), a leave balance from allowance minus approved leave. For the sample data, "stored days should equal the weekdays in the range" can be verified by generating each date and counting:
```sql
WITH RECURSIVE d AS (
  SELECT leave_request_id, start_date AS dt, end_date FROM leave_requests
  UNION ALL
  SELECT leave_request_id, dt + INTERVAL 1 DAY, end_date FROM d WHERE dt < end_date
)
SELECT lr.leave_request_id, lr.days AS stored_days, SUM(WEEKDAY(d.dt) < 5) AS weekdays
FROM   leave_requests lr
```
| JOIN   d ON d.leave_request_id = lr.leave_request_id | GROUP  BY lr.leave_request_id, lr.days |
|---|---|
| HAVING lr.days <> SUM(WEEKDAY(d.dt) < 5); | -- 0 rows: every stored value matches Monday-to-Friday counting |

(WEEKDAY() is 0 for Monday and 5 or 6 for the weekend in MySQL. Confirm the company's actual working calendar and public holidays before trusting this rule. Chapter 10.4 extends it.)
5. Current state versus history. The current status of a record should equal the last entry in its history log. When the two disagree, either the status update or the logging failed. This is the planted defect in our data:
```sql
WITH latest AS (
  SELECT h.*, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY leave_request_id ORDER BY changed_at DESC, history_id DESC) AS rn
```
| FROM   leave_status_history h | ) | SELECT lr.leave_request_id, | lr.status     AS current_status, | l.new_status  AS last_history_status, |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| CASE WHEN l.leave_request_id IS NULL THEN 'NO HISTORY' ELSE 'MISMATCH' END AS issue | FROM   leave_requests lr | LEFT JOIN latest l ON l.leave_request_id = lr.leave_request_id AND l.rn = 1 | WHERE  l.leave_request_id IS NULL OR lr.status <> l.new_status | ORDER  BY lr.leave_request_id; |

leave_request_id | current_status | last_history_status | issue
| 4                \| pending        \| NULL                \| NO HISTORY | 5                \| approved       \| NULL                \| NO HISTORY |
|---|---|
| 6                \| approved       \| NULL                \| NO HISTORY | 9                \| pending        \| approved            \| MISMATCH |

Request 9 is the serious one: the log says an approver approved it, but the request still shows pending, so either the status update failed silently or the history row was written by a different code path. Requests 4, 5 and 6 have no history at all, and whether that's a defect depends on when audit logging was introduced (older records might legitimately predate it). This is a good example of a query that produces questions as well as answers.
## Also check that the parts sum to the whole
The partition check from 2.1 and the cross-tab totals from 3.2 belong here too: bucket counts (by status, by department, by month) must add up to the grand total. When they don't, some rows have a value nobody accounted for (NULL status, a status outside the list, a department that doesn't exist).
## Assemble the checks into one scoreboard
Running individual queries is fine for exploration. For repeatable testing, combine them, as in 5.4, into one report whose rows are checks and whose numbers are violations:
```sql
SELECT 'duplicate payroll rows (employee + month)' AS check_name, COUNT(*) AS violations
FROM  (SELECT 1 FROM payroll GROUP BY employee_id, pay_month HAVING COUNT(*) > 1) x
UNION ALL
SELECT 'net pay differs from components', COUNT(*)
FROM   payroll WHERE basic_salary + allowances - deductions <> net_pay
UNION ALL
SELECT 'migrated employees loaded more than once', COUNT(*)
FROM  (SELECT 1 FROM mig_employees GROUP BY legacy_emp_no HAVING COUNT(*) > 1) x
UNION ALL
SELECT 'legacy employees missing from target', COUNT(*)
FROM   legacy_employees l LEFT JOIN mig_employees m ON m.legacy_emp_no = l.emp_no WHERE m.mig_id IS NULL
UNION ALL
SELECT 'migrated emails with stray spaces', COUNT(*)
FROM   mig_employees WHERE email <> TRIM(email)
UNION ALL
SELECT 'leave status differs from last history entry', COUNT(*)
```
| FROM   leave_requests lr | JOIN  (SELECT h.leave_request_id, h.new_status, |
|---|---|
| ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY h.leave_request_id ORDER BY h.changed_at DESC, h.history_id DESC) AS rn | FROM   leave_status_history h) l ON l.leave_request_id = lr.leave_request_id AND l.rn = 1 |
| WHERE  lr.status <> l.new_status | UNION ALL |
| SELECT 'leave requests with no history', COUNT(*) | FROM   leave_requests lr |
| WHERE  NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM leave_status_history h WHERE h.leave_request_id = lr.leave_request_id) | UNION ALL |
| SELECT 'leave requests pointing at missing employees', COUNT(*) | FROM   leave_requests lr LEFT JOIN employees e ON e.employee_id = lr.employee_id WHERE e.employee_id IS NULL; |

check_name                                     | violations
duplicate payroll rows (employee + month)      | 1
net pay differs from components                | 1
| migrated employees loaded more than once       \| 1 | legacy employees missing from target           \| 1 | migrated emails with stray spaces              \| 1 |
|---|---|---|
| leave status differs from last history entry   \| 1 | leave requests with no history                 \| 3 | leave requests pointing at missing employees   \| 0 |

Seven of eight checks fire. Each corresponds to a planted defect and each row names the rule that broke. In a real project the list grows to dozens, grouped by module (10.2).
## Interpreting results: known bad data versus new bad data
Shared QA databases always contain some pre-existing bad rows. A scoreboard that must be all zeros will be red forever, and people stop looking at red. The practical approach is to record a baseline of accepted known issues and fail only when a count goes above it: "no new orphans," "no new duplicates." That's the delta idea from 4.3. Then each new failure is caused by the change under test and points straight at the defect.
BASELINE = {   # known issues in this shared QA data set, agreed with the team
    "duplicate payroll rows (employee + month)": 1,
    "net pay differs from components": 1,
    "leave requests with no history": 3,
}

```py
def test_integrity_scoreboard(db):
| db.execute(SCOREBOARD_SQL) | failures = [(name, n, BASELINE.get(name, 0)) |
|---|---|
| for name, n in db.fetchall() if n > BASELINE.get(name, 0)] | assert not failures, f"New data-integrity violations: {failures}" |
```

## Trigger scenarios, then look
The most productive use of these queries is to run them immediately after a workflow that could break integrity: double-click Save, refresh during submit, cancel and re-apply leave, import the same file twice, delete a department with staff, deactivate a manager, approve a request from two browser tabs, retry a timed-out API call. Run the scoreboard before and after, and compare the counts. A count that went up names the workflow that caused it.

chapters.contentMarkdown:
## A schema migration changes the structure under running software
Where 6.1 moved data, a schema migration alters the database itself: adding columns, changing types, creating indexes and constraints, renaming or dropping things, and often backfilling data along the way. Most teams keep these as numbered scripts run by a tool (Flyway, Liquibase, Django, Rails, EF migrations) at every deployment. A faulty migration is nastier than a code bug, because it can lose data, block the application from starting, lock a table during business hours, or leave the database half-changed with no clean way back. As the tester you can't just click through the feature afterwards. You have to test the script itself, against realistic data, on a copy.
## Read the script first and know its risks
Before running anything, read the script and mark each statement's category:

| Statement type | What to worry about | ADD COLUMN ... NOT NULL | Needs a DEFAULT or a backfill first, or it fails on existing rows | MODIFY/ALTER COLUMN narrowing a type |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Truncation or conversion errors, silent data change | DROP COLUMN / DROP TABLE | Irreversible data loss; is anything still reading it? | RENAME | Old application code breaks immediately |
| ADD UNIQUE / ADD FOREIGN KEY / ADD CHECK | Fails if existing data already violates it | Large ALTER TABLE or CREATE INDEX | Table locks, long runtime, replication lag | UPDATE/DELETE backfills |
| Missing WHERE, huge single transaction, wrong mapping | Hard-coded IDs, names, environment values | Works in dev, wrong in staging | No guard against running twice | Second run fails halfway |

A worked example script
-- V12__leave_half_day_and_payroll_unique.sql
```sql
ALTER TABLE leave_requests ADD COLUMN is_half_day TINYINT(1) NOT NULL DEFAULT 0 AFTER days;
ALTER TABLE employees      ADD COLUMN phone VARCHAR(20) NULL AFTER email;
ALTER TABLE payroll        ADD CONSTRAINT uq_payroll_emp_month UNIQUE (employee_id, pay_month);
```

Reading it with the table above: the first two statements are safe additions (a defaulted NOT NULL column and a nullable one). The third is data-dependent, and we already know from Part 3 that payroll contains two rows for employee 2 in August 2026. Predict the failure and confirm with a pre-check query before you ever run the script:
```sql
SELECT employee_id, pay_month, COUNT(*) AS copies
FROM   payroll GROUP BY employee_id, pay_month HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;
-- 2 | 2026-08-01 | 2
```

Every constraint-adding migration deserves a pre-check like this, written from the constraint's own columns. For a foreign key, the pre-check is the orphan anti-join (4.3); for NOT NULL, WHERE col IS NULL; for a CHECK, the violation query for its condition.
Run it on a clone with realistic data, never on a shared database
```sql
Create a full copy and run there. A migration that passes on an empty dev database proves nothing, since empty tables can't violate constraints or run slowly.
```
# MySQL: copy the whole database
```sql
mysqldump -u root -p --single-transaction hrms_practice | mysql -u root -p -e "CREATE DATABASE hrms_clone"   # then load the dump into hrms_clone
```

# PostgreSQL: clone from a template (no one else may be connected to the source)
createdb -T hrms_qa hrms_qa_clone
# SQL Server: restore last night's backup under a new name

Realistic volume matters as much as realistic content: for timing, load the clone with production-sized data or the closest you can get.
## Capture a "before" fingerprint
You need something to compare with afterwards. Take a schema listing and control totals for the tables the script touches:
-- Structure before
```sql
SELECT table_name, column_name, column_type, is_nullable, column_default
FROM   information_schema.columns
WHERE  table_schema = DATABASE() AND table_name IN ('leave_requests','employees','payroll')
ORDER  BY table_name, ordinal_position;
```

-- Data before (row count plus a checksum of the existing columns)
```sql
SELECT COUNT(*) AS n,
       SUM(CRC32(CONCAT_WS('|', leave_request_id, employee_id, leave_type_id, start_date, end_date, days, status))) AS crc
FROM   leave_requests;
```

Save both results. After the migration, the same data query must return identical values, because adding a column must not change existing data.
## Run it, and watch how it fails
Execute the script statement by statement. On MySQL the first two statements succeed and the third fails:
## ERROR 1062 (23000): Duplicate entry '2-2026-08-01' for key 'payroll.uq_payroll_emp_month'

Now look at what state the database is left in. Verify with SHOW COLUMNS FROM leave_requests;, and you'll find that is_half_day and phone already exist. In MySQL every DDL statement commits implicitly (0.4), so a failed multi-statement script leaves a half-migrated database that matches neither the old nor the new version. PostgreSQL wraps DDL in transactions, so a failure would roll the whole script back, and SQL Server behaves that way only if the tool wraps the batch in a transaction. Knowing your database's behaviour tells you which recovery scenario to test.
Fix the data (the duplicate is removed in 6.6) and run the script again. It now fails at the very first line:
## ERROR 1060 (42S21): Duplicate column name 'is_half_day'

That is a finding: the script isn't idempotent or restartable. Options are ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS (PostgreSQL and MariaDB; MySQL has no such syntax), guarded checks against information_schema, or splitting one statement per script so a tool can record exactly which step succeeded. Migration tools help here, because they run each version once and record it, so check the tool's history table after each run. Flyway keeps flyway_schema_history, and Liquibase keeps DATABASECHANGELOG:
```sql
SELECT installed_rank, version, description, success
FROM   flyway_schema_history ORDER BY installed_rank;      -- illustrative output
```

installed_rank | version | description                        | success
11             | 11      | add appointment ledger             | 1
12             | 12      | leave half day and payroll unique  | 0        <-- failed, needs repair

Also check the tool's guard rails: editing an already-applied script changes its stored checksum, and the tool's validate step should then refuse to run. Out-of-order or missing versions between environments belong to 6.5.
Verify the result: structure, data, defaults, constraints
```sql
With the script fixed and applied on the clone, check four things.
```
Structure. The new columns exist with the right type, nullability and default:
```sql
SELECT table_name, column_name, column_type, is_nullable, column_default
FROM   information_schema.columns
```
| WHERE  table_schema = DATABASE() | AND ((table_name = 'leave_requests' AND column_name = 'is_half_day') |
|---|---|
| OR (table_name = 'employees'      AND column_name = 'phone')) | ORDER  BY table_name; |

table_name     | column_name | column_type | is_nullable | column_default
employees      | phone       | varchar(20) | YES         | NULL
## leave_requests | is_half_day | tinyint(1)  | NO          | 0

Existing data untouched. Re-run the "before" data query. The row count and checksum must be identical, and the new column must be filled correctly for old rows:
```sql
SELECT is_half_day, COUNT(*) AS rows_ FROM leave_requests GROUP BY is_half_day;
-- 0 | 9        every existing request got the default; nothing NULL, nothing lost
```

Constraints exist and work. Check the index metadata, then try to break it inside a rolled-back transaction, as in 4.3:
```sql
SELECT index_name, non_unique, seq_in_index, column_name
FROM   information_schema.statistics
WHERE  table_schema = DATABASE() AND index_name = 'uq_payroll_emp_month'
ORDER  BY seq_in_index;
```

index_name           | non_unique | seq_in_index | column_name
uq_payroll_emp_month | 0          | 1            | employee_id
uq_payroll_emp_month | 0          | 2            | pay_month

```sql
START TRANSACTION;
INSERT INTO payroll (employee_id, pay_month, basic_salary, allowances, deductions, net_pay)
VALUES (2, '2026-08-01', 45000, 3000, 4500, 43500);
-- ERROR 1062 (23000): Duplicate entry '2-2026-08-01' for key 'payroll.uq_payroll_emp_month'
ROLLBACK;
```

Then confirm the application handles that rejection well, by submitting a duplicate payroll run through the UI or API. A friendly message is the pass, and a raw 500 error is a defect.
Nothing else changed. Re-run the orphan scoreboard (4.3) and the schema fingerprint. The only differences from "before" should be exactly the ones the script promises.
## Data-changing migrations: the enum-rename trap
Many migrations rewrite values as well as structure, for example renaming the status inactive to deactivated. Test with a before/after count map, because every row must land in exactly one bucket:
```sql
SELECT status, COUNT(*) FROM employees GROUP BY status;
-- before: active 3 | inactive 1 | resigned 1
-- after:  active 3 | deactivated 1 | resigned 1      (no NULL, no empty string, no leftover 'inactive')
```

The dangerous implementation is a single ALTER TABLE employees MODIFY status ENUM('active','deactivated','resigned'). Existing rows holding inactive are no longer valid: strict mode raises an error, while non-strict mode converts them to an empty string (the invalid-enum marker) and you lose the information. The safe sequence is expand, migrate, contract: add deactivated to the enum (keeping inactive), UPDATE the rows, then remove inactive. A tester's job is to seed a row of every old value before running the script and check where each one ends up.
The same care applies to narrowing types. On a clone:
```sql
ALTER TABLE employees MODIFY first_name VARCHAR(5) NOT NULL;
-- strict mode:  ERROR 1265 (01000): Data truncated for column 'first_name' at row 5    ("Bikash" has 6 characters)
-- non-strict:   succeeds with a warning and silently cuts data to 5 characters
```

Compare @@sql_mode between environments, because a script can pass in one and lose data in the other (6.5).
## Compatibility with the running application (expand and contract)
During a rolling or blue/green deployment, the old application version runs against the new schema for a while, and after a rollback the previous application runs against it again. So a safe migration must work with both versions of the code:

| Change | Old code against new schema | Safe? |
|---|---|---|
| Add nullable column or column with default | Ignores it | Yes |
| Add new table | Ignores it | Yes |
| Add NOT NULL column with no default | Inserts fail | No |
| Rename or drop a column | Queries break | No, do expand then contract over two releases |
| Change a type in an incompatible way | Errors or wrong values | No |
| Add a constraint that old code violates | Inserts fail | Risky |

Test it directly: point the previous build's automated suite at the migrated database and check that everything still passes, and repeat with the new build against the pre-migration schema if rollback matters.
## Test the rollback (down) script, or the plan to roll forward
If a down script exists, test it: apply the migration, insert a little new data, run the down script, then compare the schema fingerprint to the original. Expect them to match, with one honest exception: data that lives only in the new column is gone, and anyone deploying must know that. Many teams don't roll back at all and instead fix forward with a new migration. Ask which strategy applies and test that one, including "what if the migration fails at step 3 in production?"
## Performance and locking
Run the script on a clone with production-sized data and time it. Watch whether the application stays responsive while it runs (other sessions blocked on the table, connections piling up). Whether an ALTER locks the table depends on the database and the operation: many MySQL 8 ADD COLUMN operations are instant or online (ALGORITHM=INSTANT), PostgreSQL 11 and later adds a column with a constant default without rewriting the table, while changing a column type or adding an index can lock or rewrite everything. You don't need to tune it, but you do need to report "this took 47 minutes on a production-sized copy and blocked writes."
## Smoke-test the application on the migrated database
Finish with the checks users would notice: the application starts (a mismatch between code and schema often crashes at startup), the screens that use the new columns load and save, existing records still display, and the API contract exposes the new field. A short Playwright smoke suite run against the migrated clone catches what the SQL checks can't:

| test('half-day leave saves and shows after migration', async ({ page }) => { | await page.goto('/leave/new'); | await page.getByLabel('Half day').check(); |
|---|---|---|
| await page.getByLabel('Start date').fill('2026-11-16'); | await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Submit' }).click(); | await expect(page.getByText('Leave request submitted')).toBeVisible(); |

```ts
  const [rows]: any = await db.execute(
    `SELECT is_half_day FROM leave_requests WHERE employee_id = 2 ORDER BY leave_request_id DESC LIMIT 1`);
  expect(rows[0].is_half_day).toBe(1);
});
```

| Dialect differences worth knowing | Topic | MySQL |
|---|---|---|
| PostgreSQL | SQL Server | DDL in a transaction |
| No (implicit commit) | Yes | Yes (if the batch is wrapped) |
| ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS | No | Yes |
| No (check sys.columns) | Rename a column | RENAME COLUMN (8.0+) |
| RENAME COLUMN | sp_rename | Clone for testing |
| mysqldump | CREATE DATABASE ... TEMPLATE | Restore a backup |

chapters.overviewText: Schema drift is when the structure of the database differs between environments that are supposed to match: QA, staging, UAT and production. Data drift is the same idea for reference values. The result is the classic complaint "it works in QA but breaks in staging," and it's a top source of wasted debugging days, because the code is identical and the data structure under it isn't. Typical causes: A migration ran on some environments and not others. A developer or DBA applied a hotfix by hand (a manual ALTER, an emergency index) and never wrote it into a migration. An environment was restored from an old backup. Different database versions or server settings (collation, sql_mode, time zone).

chapters.customSummary:
- Drift = structure or reference data differing between environments (missed migrations, hotfixes, old restores, direct edits, different versions/settings).
- Level 1: mysqldump --no-data / pg_dump -s and diff, or schema-compare tools (DBeaver, Redgate, Liquibase/Flyway diff, migra, Atlas).
- Level 2: compare catalog views: columns (phone only in STG, first_name 50 vs 100, enum missing inactive), indexes (unique payroll index only in STG, so QA accepts the duplicate), foreign keys (QA 3, STG 0 because LIKE doesn't copy FKs); also tables, views, triggers, procedures (compare definitions); per-dialect catalog table.
- Level 3: server settings (sql_mode, collation, charset, time zone, lower_case_table_names, group_concat_max_len, version); many "only fails in staging" bugs live here.
- Level 4: reference data drift (Annual 18 vs 20, Maternity only in STG), invisible to structural comparison; decide which side is right against the requirement.
- Automate: signature sets compared in pytest (ignore column order), scheduled and post-deployment runs, migration history comparison; beware group_concat truncation when hashing.
- On drift: determine the correct side, report as environment/process defect, fix through a migration, and re-evaluate test results obtained while environments differed.
chapters.contentMarkdown:
## What drift is and why it bites
Schema drift is when the structure of the database differs between environments that are supposed to match: QA, staging, UAT and production. Data drift is the same idea for reference values. The result is the classic complaint "it works in QA but breaks in staging," and it's a top source of wasted debugging days, because the code is identical and the data structure under it isn't. Typical causes:
A migration ran on some environments and not others.
A developer or DBA applied a hotfix by hand (a manual ALTER, an emergency index) and never wrote it into a migration.
An environment was restored from an old backup.
## Someone changed something directly in QA "to test quickly."
Different database versions or server settings (collation, sql_mode, time zone).
Reference or configuration data edited in one place only.
Our sample staging database has each of the common kinds built in. To recap, hrms_stg was created with CREATE TABLE ... LIKE, then tweaked, and only the tables employees, payroll and leave_types exist there.
## Level 1: the fast way, dump and diff
The lowest-effort comparison needs no SQL at all. Export each environment's structure without data and diff the text:
```sql
mysqldump -u qa_readonly -p --no-data --skip-comments --skip-add-drop-table hrms_qa      > qa_schema.sql
mysqldump -u qa_readonly -p --no-data --skip-comments --skip-add-drop-table hrms_staging > stg_schema.sql
```
diff qa_schema.sql stg_schema.sql

# PostgreSQL:  pg_dump --schema-only --no-owner hrms_qa > qa.sql

It is instant and complete, but noisy (auto-increment values, ordering, comments), so strip those with the dump options or a small script. Dedicated tools do the diffing better: DBeaver's schema compare, Redgate SQL Compare for SQL Server, Liquibase or Flyway diff, migra for PostgreSQL, Atlas, and SchemaCrawler. Use whichever the team already has.
## Level 2: compare catalog views with SQL
Every database describes itself in queryable catalog views (information_schema, plus vendor-specific views). When both environments live on one server, as in our example, a single query compares them. Otherwise you extract the catalog from each side and compare in code (below).
Columns. Compare the definition of every column: type, nullability, default. Column order usually doesn't matter, so exclude it:
```sql
WITH q AS (
  SELECT table_name, column_name, column_type, is_nullable, column_default
  FROM   information_schema.columns
  WHERE  table_schema = 'hrms_practice' AND table_name IN ('employees','payroll','leave_types')),
s AS (
  SELECT table_name, column_name, column_type, is_nullable, column_default
  FROM   information_schema.columns
  WHERE  table_schema = 'hrms_stg' AND table_name IN ('employees','payroll','leave_types'))
SELECT 'only in QA' AS drift, q.table_name, q.column_name, q.column_type AS qa_value, NULL AS stg_value
FROM   q LEFT JOIN s ON s.table_name = q.table_name AND s.column_name = q.column_name
WHERE  s.column_name IS NULL
UNION ALL
SELECT 'only in STG', s.table_name, s.column_name, NULL, s.column_type
FROM   s LEFT JOIN q ON q.table_name = s.table_name AND q.column_name = s.column_name
WHERE  q.column_name IS NULL
UNION ALL
SELECT 'definition differs', q.table_name, q.column_name, q.column_type, s.column_type
FROM   q JOIN s ON s.table_name = q.table_name AND s.column_name = q.column_name
WHERE  NOT (q.column_type <=> s.column_type AND q.is_nullable <=> s.is_nullable
        AND q.column_default <=> s.column_default)
ORDER  BY table_name, column_name;
```

drift              | table_name | column_name | qa_value                             | stg_value
only in STG        | employees  | phone       | NULL                                 | varchar(20)
definition differs | employees  | first_name  | varchar(50)                          | varchar(100)
definition differs | employees  | status      | enum('active','inactive','resigned') | enum('active','resigned')

The three drifts have three different consequences. phone exists only in staging, so a build that reads it works in staging and crashes in QA. first_name is 50 characters in QA and 100 in staging, so a 70-character name passes in staging and fails (or is truncated) in QA. The status enum in staging lacks inactive, so deactivating an employee works in QA and errors in staging. Each is a defect report waiting to be written, and each one shows why "passed in QA" alone means less than it seems.
Indexes and unique constraints. A missing unique index is a correctness difference. A missing ordinary index is a performance difference. Compare index definitions the same way:
```sql
WITH q AS (
  SELECT table_name, index_name, GROUP_CONCAT(column_name ORDER BY seq_in_index) AS cols
  FROM   information_schema.statistics
  WHERE  table_schema = 'hrms_practice' AND table_name IN ('employees','payroll','leave_types')
  GROUP  BY table_name, index_name),
s AS (
  SELECT table_name, index_name, GROUP_CONCAT(column_name ORDER BY seq_in_index) AS cols
  FROM   information_schema.statistics
  WHERE  table_schema = 'hrms_stg' AND table_name IN ('employees','payroll','leave_types')
  GROUP  BY table_name, index_name)
SELECT COALESCE(q.table_name, s.table_name) AS table_name,
```
| COALESCE(q.index_name, s.index_name) AS index_name, | q.cols AS qa_columns, s.cols AS stg_columns |
|---|---|
| FROM   q LEFT JOIN s ON s.table_name = q.table_name AND s.index_name = q.index_name | WHERE  s.index_name IS NULL OR NOT (q.cols <=> s.cols) |
| UNION ALL | SELECT s.table_name, s.index_name, NULL, s.cols |
| FROM   s LEFT JOIN q ON q.table_name = s.table_name AND q.index_name = s.index_name | WHERE  q.index_name IS NULL; |

table_name | index_name           | qa_columns | stg_columns
## payroll    | uq_payroll_emp_month | NULL       | employee_id,pay_month

Staging already has the payroll uniqueness rule, and QA doesn't. So QA is the environment that accepts the duplicate August payroll row, while staging would have rejected it. That is the same defect story from Parts 3 and 6.4, now seen as drift: the very bug you found in QA can't happen in staging, so it will never be caught there, while the migration that adds the constraint will fail in QA and pass in staging. Both directions matter.
Foreign keys. List them per environment:
```sql
SELECT constraint_schema, table_name, constraint_name, referenced_table_name
FROM   information_schema.referential_constraints
WHERE  constraint_schema IN ('hrms_practice','hrms_stg') AND table_name IN ('employees','payroll')
ORDER  BY constraint_schema, table_name, constraint_name;
```

constraint_schema | table_name | constraint_name   | referenced_table_name
| hrms_practice     \| employees  \| employees_ibfk_1  \| departments | hrms_practice     \| employees  \| employees_ibfk_2  \| employees |
|---|---|
| hrms_practice     \| payroll    \| payroll_ibfk_1    \| employees | (no rows for hrms_stg) |

QA enforces three relationships and staging enforces none. Cause: CREATE TABLE ... LIKE copies columns and indexes but not foreign keys, which is also a realistic way for a hand-built environment to lose them. The consequence is that orphans can be created freely in staging (4.3), and the tests that expect a rejected delete will behave differently there.
Everything else. The same approach compares other object types. Which catalog view to use differs per database:

| Object | MySQL | PostgreSQL | SQL Server |
|---|---|---|---|
| Tables | information_schema.tables | information_schema.tables | sys.tables |
| Columns | information_schema.columns | information_schema.columns | sys.columns |
| Indexes | information_schema.statistics | pg_indexes | sys.indexes |
| Constraints | table_constraints, key_column_usage | pg_constraint | sys.check_constraints, sys.foreign_keys |
| Views | information_schema.views | information_schema.views | sys.views |
| Triggers | information_schema.triggers | information_schema.triggers | sys.triggers |
| Procedures/functions | information_schema.routines | information_schema.routines | sys.procedures |

For views, triggers and procedures, compare the definition text too, because the same name with different logic is drift that a name check misses. And a whole-table check that runs first is SELECT table_name FROM information_schema.tables WHERE table_schema = ... on each side, using the same LEFT JOIN ... IS NULL idea.
## Level 3: server settings and environment behaviour
Identical structure can still behave differently because the server is configured differently. Compare these and note every difference:
```sql
-- MySQL
SELECT @@version, @@sql_mode, @@collation_server, @@character_set_server, @@time_zone,
       @@lower_case_table_names, @@group_concat_max_len;
-- PostgreSQL:  SHOW server_version;  SHOW timezone;  SHOW lc_collate;  SHOW standard_conforming_strings;
-- SQL Server:  SELECT @@VERSION, SERVERPROPERTY('Collation'); SELECT name, compatibility_level FROM sys.databases;
```

Earlier chapters told you why each matters: sql_mode decides whether GROUP BY shortcuts and silent truncation are allowed (1.2, 3.2), the collation decides case and trailing-space matching and sort order (2.5), the time zone shifts attendance punches (1.2), lower_case_table_names makes a query work on Windows and fail on Linux (1.1), and group_concat_max_len cuts off concatenated lists (2.4). A test that "only fails in staging" is very often one of these.
## Level 4: reference data drift
Lookup and configuration tables (leave types, allowance rules, statuses, roles, tax slabs, feature flags) should be the same in every environment unless a difference is deliberate. Compare them by key, with the three-way classification from 6.2:
```sql
SELECT q.leave_type_id, q.name, q.days_per_year AS qa_days, s.days_per_year AS stg_days,
       CASE WHEN s.leave_type_id IS NULL THEN 'ONLY IN QA' ELSE 'VALUE DIFFERS' END AS result
```
| FROM   hrms_practice.leave_types q | LEFT JOIN hrms_stg.leave_types s ON s.leave_type_id = q.leave_type_id |
|---|---|
| WHERE  s.leave_type_id IS NULL OR NOT (q.name <=> s.name AND q.days_per_year <=> s.days_per_year) | UNION ALL |
| SELECT s.leave_type_id, s.name, NULL, s.days_per_year, 'ONLY IN STG' | FROM   hrms_stg.leave_types s |
| LEFT JOIN hrms_practice.leave_types q ON q.leave_type_id = s.leave_type_id | WHERE  q.leave_type_id IS NULL; |

leave_type_id | name      | qa_days | stg_days | result
1             | Annual    | 18      | 20       | VALUE DIFFERS
3             | Maternity | NULL    | 98       | ONLY IN STG

This is the sneakiest drift, because the structure is identical and every schema comparison passes. Yet annual leave is 18 days in QA and 20 in staging, so every leave-balance test yields different expected numbers per environment, and the Maternity type can't be tested at all in QA. When reference data differs, check which environment is correct against the requirement before filing anything.
## Turning the checks into an automated gate
Drift is cheapest to catch continuously. When the environments are on different servers, fetch each catalog into a set and compare:

| def schema_signature(conn, schema): | with conn.cursor() as cur: |
|---|---|
| cur.execute(""" | SELECT table_name, column_name, column_type, is_nullable, IFNULL(column_default, '<NULL>') |
| FROM   information_schema.columns | WHERE  table_schema = %s |
| ORDER  BY table_name, ordinal_position""", (schema,)) | return {tuple(r) for r in cur.fetchall()}        # a set ignores column order on purpose |

```py
def test_qa_and_staging_schemas_match(qa_conn, stg_conn):
    qa, stg = schema_signature(qa_conn, "hrms_qa"), schema_signature(stg_conn, "hrms_staging")
    assert qa == stg, (f"Only in QA:  {sorted(qa - stg)}\n"
                       f"Only in STG: {sorted(stg - qa)}")
```

Add the same for indexes, foreign keys and reference-data tables. Run it as a scheduled job, and again right after every deployment, and post the failing lines to the team channel. Also compare the migration history table (flyway_schema_history) between environments. If QA is at version 12 and staging at 10, you have found the drift's cause before comparing a single column. If you hash a whole catalog listing into one fingerprint, remember group_concat_max_len (2.4), or the "fingerprint" will silently be computed over a truncated string.
## What to do when you find drift
Work out which side is right (the migration scripts or the design decide, not whichever environment you happened to test first). Then file it as an environment or process defect, with the exact statements that show the difference, and fix it through a migration (6.4) and never by hand-editing one environment, or the next drift is already in progress. Record which of your earlier test results are now in doubt: anything that ran while the environments differed may have passed or failed for the wrong reason.

chapters.title: 6.6 Before/After Snapshot (Regression) Validation
chapters.overviewText: Many changes should alter some data and leave everything else exactly as it was: a payroll recalculation, a release, a data-fix script, a bulk update, a migration, a "cleanup" job, an upgrade of the database version. Every difference must be one the change is supposed to cause. If you know Playwright's toHaveScreenshot() or Jest snapshots, it's the same workflow applied to data: baseline, action, compare, review the diff, accept or reject. chapters.customSummary:
- Capture, act, compare: like toHaveScreenshot() for data; every difference must be one the change is meant to cause.
- Snapshot with CREATE TABLE ... AS SELECT, CSV export, temp table or saved results; limit to your data slice; keep aggregates plus rows; use a consistent-read transaction on busy databases.
- Diff by primary key into CHANGED / REMOVED / ADDED with NULL-safe comparison (found the two announced changes and two silent ones: row 1 status, extra row 9).
- Compare against an allow-list of expected changes; extend to column level ("only net_pay may change").
- Aggregate before/after (count and total by status) gives the headline (total +24,500 instead of the expected small net change).
- Make it robust: exclude volatile columns, total ordering, wait for async jobs, isolate your slice, change nothing else in between.
- Automate with baselines in the repo or snapshot-style assertions (added, removed, changed columns).
- Applications: upgrades, idempotency (second run gives empty diff), rollback, bulk operations, cleanup jobs, report regressions.
- Cleanup script restores payroll from the snapshot, removes Part 6 objects, and keeps leave_status_history for Part 7.

## The idea: capture, act, compare
Many changes should alter some data and leave everything else exactly as it was: a payroll recalculation, a release, a data-fix script, a bulk update, a migration, a "cleanup" job, an upgrade of the database version. A snapshot check makes that promise testable. Take a snapshot of the relevant data before, perform the action, take a snapshot after, and diff them. Every difference must be one the change is supposed to cause. If you know Playwright's toHaveScreenshot() or Jest snapshots, it's the same workflow applied to data: baseline, action, compare, review the diff, accept or reject.
Step 1: take the snapshot
The simplest snapshot is a copy of the table:
```sql
CREATE TABLE snap_payroll_before AS SELECT * FROM payroll;
```

Other ways, depending on permissions and size: export the rows to CSV (11.3) and diff the files; SELECT ... INTO OUTFILE; PostgreSQL's COPY (SELECT ...) TO; a temporary table for the length of your session; or, on a read-only account, run a saved query before and after and store both result sets outside the database. For a large table, snapshot only the slice you care about (your tagged test data, one month, one department) and keep aggregates as well as rows. Comparing every row is best; comparing rows plus a handful of control totals is the practical middle.
On a shared, busy database, other people's writes will appear in your diff. Snapshot only the rows your test owns, or take the snapshot inside a consistent-read transaction (START TRANSACTION WITH CONSISTENT SNAPSHOT; in MySQL, REPEATABLE READ isolation in others; see 7.7).
## Step 2: perform the action
Here the "release" is a fix script. The developer says it corrects one payroll row and removes the duplicate, and nothing else. Simulated below, including two side effects that the developer didn't mention. The explicit payroll_id of 9 avoids depending on the auto-increment counter:
```sql
UPDATE payroll SET net_pay = 67000 WHERE payroll_id = 3;      -- intended: fix the underpaid row
DELETE FROM payroll WHERE payroll_id = 7;                     -- intended: remove the duplicate
```

```sql
UPDATE payroll SET status = 'paid' WHERE payroll_id = 1;      -- side effect nobody mentioned
INSERT INTO payroll (payroll_id, employee_id, pay_month, basic_salary, allowances, deductions, net_pay, status)
VALUES (9, 3, '2026-09-01', 70000, 6000, 9000, 67000, 'draft');   -- another side effect
```

## Step 3: diff, keyed by primary key
Classify every row as CHANGED, REMOVED or ADDED, with a NULL-safe comparison on every column:
```sql
SELECT 'CHANGED' AS change_type, b.payroll_id,
```
| b.net_pay AS before_net, a.net_pay AS after_net, | b.status  AS before_status, a.status AS after_status | FROM   snap_payroll_before b |
|---|---|---|
| JOIN   payroll a ON a.payroll_id = b.payroll_id | WHERE  NOT (b.employee_id <=> a.employee_id AND b.pay_month <=> a.pay_month | AND b.basic_salary <=> a.basic_salary AND b.allowances <=> a.allowances |
| AND b.deductions <=> a.deductions AND b.net_pay <=> a.net_pay AND b.status <=> a.status) | UNION ALL | SELECT 'REMOVED', b.payroll_id, b.net_pay, NULL, b.status, NULL |
| FROM   snap_payroll_before b | LEFT JOIN payroll a ON a.payroll_id = b.payroll_id | WHERE  a.payroll_id IS NULL |
| UNION ALL | SELECT 'ADDED', a.payroll_id, NULL, a.net_pay, NULL, a.status | FROM   payroll a |
| LEFT JOIN snap_payroll_before b ON b.payroll_id = a.payroll_id | WHERE  b.payroll_id IS NULL | ORDER  BY payroll_id; |

| change_type \| payroll_id \| before_net \| after_net \| before_status \| after_status | CHANGED     \| 1          \| 57500.00   \| 57500.00  \| processed     \| paid |
|---|---|
| CHANGED     \| 3          \| 66000.00   \| 67000.00  \| draft         \| draft | REMOVED     \| 7          \| 43500.00   \| NULL      \| processed     \| NULL |

Four differences, and the developer only announced two. Rows 3 and 7 are the intended fix and dedupe. Row 1's status silently moved from processed to paid (a payment marker that could trigger a bank file), and row 9 is a September payroll record nobody asked for. These are exactly the kind of collateral changes users discover a month later, and a plain "it fixed the row I was told about" test never finds them. The three counts also correspond to the three classic mistakes: an over-broad UPDATE, an unintended INSERT, and a missing WHERE.
## Step 4: compare against the allow-list of expected changes
Diffing produces facts, and the judgement is "were these expected?" Encode the expectations as a small table and subtract them:
```sql
CREATE TABLE expected_changes (change_type VARCHAR(10), payroll_id INT);
INSERT INTO expected_changes VALUES ('CHANGED', 3), ('REMOVED', 7);
```

```sql
WITH diff AS ( /* the UNION ALL diff query above */ )
```
| SELECT d.* | FROM   diff d |
|---|---|
| LEFT JOIN expected_changes x ON x.change_type = d.change_type AND x.payroll_id = d.payroll_id | WHERE  x.payroll_id IS NULL; |

## change_type | payroll_id | before_net | after_net | before_status | after_status
## CHANGED     | 1          | 57500.00   | 57500.00  | processed     | paid
## ADDED       | 9          | NULL       | 67000.00  | NULL          | draft

An empty result means "the change did exactly what it promised." Anything left is a defect or a requirement conversation. For sharper checks, the allow-list can go to column level ("only net_pay may change on row 3"), since row 3's status changing as well would slip through at row level.
## Step 5: aggregate snapshots (control totals before and after)
Row diffs are precise but can be huge. Aggregates give the headline. Keep a "before" summary and compare it with an "after" summary, which also matches what a dashboard would show:
```sql
WITH b AS (SELECT status, COUNT(*) AS n, SUM(net_pay) AS total FROM snap_payroll_before GROUP BY status),
     a AS (SELECT status, COUNT(*) AS n, SUM(net_pay) AS total FROM payroll             GROUP BY status)
SELECT b.status,
       b.n AS n_before, a.n AS n_after, a.n - b.n AS n_change,
       b.total AS total_before, a.total AS total_after, a.total - b.total AS total_change
FROM   b JOIN a ON a.status = b.status
ORDER  BY b.status;
```

## status    | n_before | n_after | n_change | total_before | total_after | total_change
## draft     | 1        | 2       | 1        | 66000.00     | 134000.00   | 68000.00
## paid      | 3        | 4       | 1        | 168000.00    | 225500.00   | 57500.00
## processed | 3        | 1       | -2       | 144500.00    | 43500.00    | -101000.00

The grand totals moved from 378,500 to 403,000, up by 24,500, which is what +68000 + 57500 - 101000 gives. The story to test against the requirement is "the release should change the grand total by exactly +1,000 (the corrected row) minus 43,500 (the duplicate)", and instead a whole extra payroll row and a status change inflated it. (The join assumes each status exists on both sides. If a status could appear on only one side, use the full-outer pattern from 4.1.)
Step 6: make the comparison robust
## Snapshot comparisons fail for boring reasons unless you plan for them:
Volatile columns. Exclude or normalise created_at, updated_at, generated UUIDs and auto-increment values that legitimately change on every run, or your diff drowns in noise.
Stable ordering. Sort with a total order before comparing exported lists (2.2).
Timing. Asynchronous jobs, message queues and scheduled tasks may still be changing data when you take the "after" snapshot, so wait for them to finish and check that the counts have settled.
Isolation. Other testers and automation jobs write to shared data. Snapshot only what you own, or use a dedicated slice.
Same everything else. The action should be the only change between the two snapshots, so don't refresh data or deploy anything else in between.
```sql
Use it as an automated regression check
```
For a repeatable suite, run the same "golden queries" before and after every release or environment upgrade, store the "before" results as approved baselines in the repository, and fail the pipeline on any unexplained difference. In test code, it looks like a snapshot assertion:

```ts
test('payroll recalculation only changes the corrected row', async () => {
  const before = await db.query(SNAPSHOT_SQL);              // sorted, volatile columns left out
  await runPayrollRecalculation({ month: '2026-08' });
  const after  = await db.query(SNAPSHOT_SQL);
```

```ts
  expect(changed.added).toEqual([]);
| expect(changed.removed.map(r => r.payroll_id)).toEqual([7]); | expect(changed.changed.map(c => c.key)).toEqual([3]); |

| expect(changed.changed[0].columns).toEqual(['net_pay']);   // and only this column | }); |
```

## Where else this technique applies
Upgrades and version changes: run the same queries on the old and new database version and diff; look for changed collation behaviour, changed rounding, changed GROUP BY output order (3.2).
Idempotency: run a job twice and confirm the second run produces an empty diff.
```sql
Rollback testing: snapshot, apply, roll back, and check the diff against the original is empty.
```
Bulk operations: an approval of many requests, a mass status change, a data import; the diff must contain only the selected records.
Cleanup jobs: verify that archived or deleted rows are the intended ones and that their dependants (4.3) are handled.
Reports: save the report's numbers before and after a code change that "shouldn't affect the output."
